step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 21-year-old female traveler from Luanda, Angola, evaluated for high fever

step5_concept_grounding: Yellow fever virus evaluated as differential diagnosis during ongoing outbreak in Angola and ruled out

evidence_items.source_quote: Although the patient was supposedly vaccinated against yellow fever virus, we performed real-time reverse transcription PCR for yellow fever virus, and the result was confirmed to be negative.
evidence_items.test_name: real-time reverse transcription PCR for yellow fever virus

evidence_items.source_quote: Testing for other arboviruses was performed, and real-time reverse transcription PCR for chikungunya virus (CHIKV) showed a positive result. Therefore, the final diagnosis was chikungunya fever.
evidence_items.test_name: real-time reverse transcription PCR for chikungunya virus

rationale: A 21-year-old female traveler from Luanda, Angola, presented to a hospital in Tokyo with high fever during an ongoing yellow fever outbreak in Angola. Yellow fever virus real-time reverse transcription PCR was performed to evaluate the differential diagnosis and was confirmed negative. An alternative pathogen (chikungunya virus) was detected by RT-PCR, establishing chikungunya fever as the definitive diagnosis. Target disease was explicitly tested and ruled out. VPD = false -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 45-year-old male traveler returning to the UK from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

evidence_items.source_quote: Results of serologic testing for chikungunya, dengue, and yellow fever were negative by commercial assays.
evidence_items.test_name: Commercial serologic assay for Yellow fever

evidence_items.source_quote: On day 3 of his illness, Zika virus RNA was detected in urine but not in serum

step10_contradiction_notes: No contradiction; yellow fever serology was negative and Zika virus infection was confirmed by urine/semen rRT-PCR and convalescent serology.
rationale: A 45-year-old man returning to the UK from Brazil presented with fever, retro-orbital headache, arthralgia, myalgia, and rash. Commercial serologic testing for yellow fever on day 3 was explicitly negative, whereas Zika virus RNA was detected in urine and serial semen samples (up to day 92) with Zika IgM/IgG seroconversion at day 20. Yellow fever was ruled out in the differential workup -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: Two concurrent adult male patients in Central African Republic: Patient 1 (28yo male bitten by squirrel) and Patient 2 (26yo male farmer) in whom Yellow Fever virus infection was explicitly ruled out

step4_condition_matched: Yellow Fever virus infection (hemorrhagic fever differential workup)

evidence_items.source_quote: Filo-, Yellow Fever and Dengue virus infections were ruled out.
evidence_items.test_name: Reference laboratory viral hemorrhagic fever testing

step10_contradiction_notes: Yellow Fever virus infection was explicitly tested for at the regional reference laboratory in Bangui and ruled out.
rationale: This report describes two concurrent adult males (ages 28 and 26) in the Central African Republic presenting with fever, myalgia, vesiculo-bullous skin lesions, and transient hemorrhage (epistaxis, hematemesis/bloody stools). Because hemorrhagic fever etiologies were considered alongside suspected monkeypox, blood samples were sent to the reference laboratory in Bangui, where 'Filo-, Yellow Fever and Dengue virus infections were ruled out.' Yellow Fever was explicitly excluded -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 49-year-old female presenting with fulminant myocarditis and cardiogenic shock

step4_condition_matched: Yellow fever virus (broad viral myocarditis etiology workup)

evidence_items.source_quote: Blood and biopsy specimens were tested for common causative agents, such as Coxsackieviruses A and B, echoviruses, polioviruses, influenza A and B viruses, respiratory syncytial virus, mumps virus, measles virus, rubella virus, hepatitis C virus, dengue virus, yellow fever virus, Chikungunya virus, human immunodeficiency virus-1, adenoviruses, parvovirus B19, cytomegalovirus, human herpes virus-6, Epstein-Barr virus, varicella-zoster virus, and herpes simplex virus, as recommended, but none of these triggers was detected.
evidence_items.test_name: Viral PCR / microbiological panel on blood and endomyocardial biopsy

evidence_items.source_quote: Viral PCR (polymerase chain reaction) in RNA-stabilized EMB and EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) blood demonstrated absence of infectious causative organisms.
evidence_items.target_concept: Infectious viral agents including Yellow fever virus
evidence_items.specimen: RNA-stabilized endomyocardial biopsy and EDTA blood

step10_contradiction_notes: Yellow fever virus was tested in blood and endomyocardial biopsy specimens and explicitly not detected.
rationale: A 49-year-old woman presented with fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis and cardiogenic shock requiring Impella CP support. Blood and endomyocardial biopsy specimens were tested by viral PCR for a broad panel of pathogens including yellow fever virus, and 'none of these triggers was detected.' Because yellow fever virus was explicitly tested and negative, the case is adjudicated as NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 29-year-old female cemetery cleaner in urban Rio de Janeiro

step4_condition_matched: Yellow fever (differential diagnosis and serologic workup)

evidence_items.source_quote: Other hypotheses covered dengue, yellow fever, prolonged septicemic salmonellosis, brucellosis, malaria, Chagas disease and lymphoproliferative malignancies. An evaluation by thick and thin blood smear, blood culture, stool tests, bone marrow biopsy and aspiration and serology for dengue, yellow fever, brucellosis and Chagas disease were requested.
The bone marrow aspirate confirmed the presence of Leishmania amastigotes (Fig. 2).

step10_contradiction_notes: Yellow fever was initially listed among broad differential hypotheses and serology was requested, but bone marrow aspirate definitively confirmed visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania amastigotes) with full clinical resolution on amphotericin B.
rationale: A 29-year-old woman in Rio de Janeiro presented with a 5-month history of intermittent fever, weight loss, cholestatic jaundice, massive hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. Yellow fever was included as an initial differential diagnostic hypothesis and serology was requested, but bone marrow aspirate confirmed Leishmania amastigotes (visceral leishmaniasis), and the patient recovered with amphotericin B therapy. Because yellow fever was considered only in the differential diagnosis and ruled out by definitive confirmation of visceral leishmaniasis, it is adjudicated as NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 25-year-old male farmer admitted to a mission hospital in western Kenya

step4_condition_matched: Yellow fever virus (IgM capture ELISA and flavivirus RT-PCR in VHF workup)

evidence_items.source_quote: Serologic tests in Nairobi were negative for yellow fever, dengue, West Nile, Chikungunya, and Rift Valley fever (immunoglobulin [Ig] M-capture enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) and reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) tests for flaviviruses, alphaviruses, and Bunyamwera serogroup bunyaviruses were also negative.
evidence_items.test_name: IgM-capture ELISA for yellow fever and flavivirus RT-PCR

evidence_items.source_quote: RT-PCR for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (C-CHFV) was positive.

step10_contradiction_notes: Yellow fever was explicitly tested by IgM-capture ELISA and flavivirus RT-PCR and found negative; Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (C-CHFV) was confirmed by RT-PCR and amplicon sequencing.
rationale: A 25-year-old male farmer in western Kenya died of an acute hemorrhagic fever. Diagnostic testing of serum at the reference laboratory in Nairobi was explicitly negative for yellow fever by IgM-capture ELISA and negative for flaviviruses by RT-PCR, whereas RT-PCR and sequencing confirmed Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (C-CHFV) in both Nairobi and Johannesburg. Yellow fever was definitively ruled out -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 32-year-old Brazilian white male returning to Campinas, Brazil from South Africa

step4_condition_matched: Yellow fever serology (acute febrile traveler differential workup)

evidence_items.source_quote: Whole blood and blood clot were collected (in BHI solution and frozen at -70 C) for microbiological procedures and serum samples for serological tests (spotted fever group rickettsiae, dengue, yellow fever, leptospirosis), malaria and dengue-NS1 point-of-care rapid tests.
All the other serological tests, and antigen detection (for malaria and dengue-NS1) and routine blood cultures were negative.
evidence_items.test_name: Serological panel including yellow fever, dengue, and leptospirosis

step10_contradiction_notes: Yellow fever serology was explicitly negative; Rickettsia africae (African tick-bite fever) was confirmed by seroconversion, Vero cell culture isolation, and PCR/sequencing.
rationale: A 32-year-old Brazilian traveler returning from South Africa presented with fever, headache, myalgia, maculopapular rash, inguinal lymphadenopathy, and a necrotic eschar. Serum samples were tested for spotted fever group rickettsiae, dengue, yellow fever, and leptospirosis; while Rickettsia spp. IgG seroconverted and Rickettsia africae was isolated in culture and confirmed by PCR/sequencing, 'All the other serological tests, and antigen detection (for malaria and dengue-NS1) and routine blood cultures were negative.' Yellow fever was tested and ruled out -> NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 40-year-old male traveler from Bangladesh admitted to Nakasero Hospital in Uganda (Case report 1, ARB01183/Uganda)

step4_condition_matched: Yellow fever virus (IgM capture ELISA and flavivirus RT-PCR in arboviral workup, plus prior travel vaccination)

evidence_items.source_quote: The patient had no significant past medical history, was on no regular medication, and had received yellow fever specific travel-related vaccination.

A total of 284 serum samples collected in 2017 were tested for yellow virus (YFV), West Nile virus (WNV), DENV1-4, CHIKV and Zika virus (ZIKV) antibodies by IgM capture ELISA. Only the diagnostic testing results for arbovirus infections of the three travel-related cases are shown and summarized in Table 1. All serological testing in case report 1 (ARB01183/Uganda) were negative, while high neutralizing antibodies against DENV2 were found for both sisters that traveled to Ethiopia in case report 2 (ARB01227UVRI and ARB01228UVRI).
RNA extracted from harvested virus supernatant and tested by group-specific RT-PCR was positive for alphavirus and negative for flavivirus and bunyavirus.
evidence_items.test_name: Group-specific flavivirus RT-PCR on Vero cell culture supernatant

step10_contradiction_notes: Patient had prior yellow fever travel vaccination and tested negative for YFV IgM by ELISA and negative for flavivirus RNA by RT-PCR; Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) was isolated and confirmed by RT-PCR and whole-genome sequencing.
rationale: A 40-year-old male traveling from Bangladesh to the DRC via Uganda presented with acute fever and joint pain. He had previously received yellow fever travel vaccination. Acute serum testing at the Uganda Virus Research Institute (UVRI) was explicitly negative for yellow fever virus (YFV) IgM by capture ELISA, and viral culture supernatant was negative for flavivirus by group-specific RT-PCR, whereas Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) was confirmed by real-time RT-PCR and next-generation sequencing. Because Yellow Fever was directly tested and ruled out, the case is adjudicated as NEGATIVE.

step3_patient_anchor.coreference_notes: 65-year-old Canadian-born male from southern Ontario returning from a 12-day trip to Ecuador and the Galapagos Islands

step4_condition_matched: Yellow Fever serology (post-travel febrile and cranial neuropathy differential workup)

evidence_items.source_quote: A broad infectious work up, including blood and urine cultures, respiratory virus PCR, malaria thick and thin blood smear and rapid diagnostic test, and serologic testing for Hepatitis A, B, C, and E, Dengue virus, Chikungunya virus, West Nile virus, Yellow Fever, Rickettsia (spotted fever and typhi), and Trypanosome cruzi, were negative.

Shortly after his clinic visit, the Borrelia burgdorferi serologic testing performed during his first visit to the ED was reported as reactive (tier 1 IgG/IgM ELISA: reactive; tier 2 anti-VlsE1+pepC10 IgG/IgM ELISA: reactive), confirming a diagnosis of Lyme disease.
evidence_items.test_name: Modified two-tier testing (MTTT) Borrelia burgdorferi serology

step10_contradiction_notes: Serologic testing for Yellow Fever was explicitly negative; acute Lyme neuroborreliosis was confirmed by modified two-tier Borrelia burgdorferi serology and complete clinical response to doxycycline.
rationale: A 65-year-old Canadian man returning from Ecuador presented with fever, erythema migrans rash, and cranial nerve VII and XII palsies. Because of his tropical travel history, a comprehensive infectious workup was performed, and serologic testing for Yellow Fever was explicitly negative. Modified two-tier serologic testing for Borrelia burgdorferi was reactive, confirming acute Lyme neuroborreliosis, and his symptoms resolved completely after a 4-week course of doxycycline. Yellow Fever was explicitly tested and ruled out -> NEGATIVE.
